sections.history: Tirukkanur lies on the bank of the Kollidam in Thanjavur district, a few kilometres from Tirukkattupalli, and is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the Shiva temples north of the Kaveri praised in the Tevaram by Sambandar and Appar. Appar's hymn describes the form of the Lord of Kanur, and the name of the presiding deity, Semmeninathar, the Lord of the red body, recalls that radiant form. The locality is also called Manalmedu, the sandy mound, a name that speaks of the river that has shaped this place. Tradition links the site with the early Chola king Karikala, though the patrons of the present structure are not firmly known. Remote and little changed, it remains a place of quiet, steady worship.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is modest in scale, entered beneath a two-tiered rajagopuram whose ceiling carries carved reliefs of the solar and lunar eclipses. The sanctum of Semmeninathar holds the linga, honoured as swayambhu, self-manifested. The goddess Sivayoga Nayaki has her own shrine facing south, crowned by a vesara-style vimana. Beyond the walls, the Kollidam and open fields give the temple a setting of rare stillness, far from the crowds of the larger Kaveri shrines.
sections.legends: Three old traditions gather at Tirukkanur. In one, the goddess Parvati performed penance at this place, and Shiva appeared before her as a blazing fire, red as flame, and so came to be called Semmeninathar, the red-bodied Lord. In another, the sage Parasurama worshipped Shiva here to be freed from the burden of his deeds as a warrior. The third is the story of the sugarcane: the temple, it is said, lay hidden beneath drifted river sand until a shepherd came upon it, with a single sugarcane growing from the spot. From karumbu, the Tamil word for sugarcane, the Lord is also called Karumbeswarar. Each is a tradition of the place and is told as such.
sections.festivals: The most distinctive observance here is the sun's own worship. In the Tamil month of Panguni, around the first days of April, the morning rays are reported to fall on the linga for about three days, and the temple keeps these as a festival of Surya's homage. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Tirukkanur is for those who prefer solitude to spectacle. The temple is small, the road ends in a rough track, and the priest comes from the nearby town, so plan the visit in daylight and arrange it beforehand. Offer prayers to Semmeninathar, then to Sivayoga Nayaki in her south-facing shrine, and look up at the eclipse reliefs on the gopuram ceiling. If the day is clear, linger by the Kollidam; the sandy ground and the open sky explain why the place was once called Manalmedu.

visit.timings: Reported hours are a short morning window (about 10:00 to 11:30) and a late-afternoon window (about 3:30 to 5:00). The priest travels from Tirukkattupalli, so contact him or the temple in advance and confirm timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer areas but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask the priest before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukkanur stands on the bank of the Kollidam in Thanjavur district, about 6 km from Tirukkattupalli, which is as far as the buses go. From there, hire an auto-rickshaw or car; the last stretch is an unpaved road, so a daylight visit is advised. Budhalur is the nearest listed railway station, and Tiruchirappalli the nearest airport.
